mainTopic: The snake's seven-year pregnancy, and רבי יהושע בן חנניה's contest of wits with the elders of Athens
overview: The amud starts by defending how the גמרא learned from the curse of the נחש that a snake carries its young for seven years. The verse lists בהמה before חיה. This sets up a chain: the snake is cursed more than the בהמה, which was cursed more than the חיה. The גמרא asks why the ratio should not be the goat's one to three, which would give only fifteen months. It answers in two ways: 'from all the בהמה' includes the donkey, the most cursed one, and a curse is read at its harshest. Then comes a story. The קיסר challenges רבי יהושע בן חנניה's answer of seven years with an experiment by the elders of Athens. רבי יהושע defends it and claims the Jewish sages are wiser. Dared to prove it, he travels to Athens, tricks his way into their guarded school, and wins a contest of riddles and impossible demands, mostly by answering absurdity with absurdity. Finally he brings the sixty sages onto his ship and sets sail with earth from Athens, and the story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse's word order shows a chain of curses
steps.stepSummary: The verse lists בהמה first and חיה second. This teaches that the snake was cursed more than the בהמה, which had itself been cursed more than the חיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it written 'from all the wild animals and from all the domesticated animals'? No, it is written 'from all the domesticated animals and from all the wild animals'! This means the snake is cursed more than the domesticated animal, which was itself cursed more than the wild animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is defending its earlier reading of the verse. It points out that the verse names בהמה first and חיה second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word order sets up a chain of three: חיה, then בהמה, then the snake. The בהמה's curse is measured against the חיה. The snake's curse is then measured against the בהמה. So the snake's seven years come from multiplying the בהמה's gestation, not the חיה's.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written...? (a rhetorical way of saying the verse does not say that)
Domesticated animal (like a donkey or goat)
Was cursed (here: given a longer pregnancy)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Cursed' here is measured by how long an animal carries its young. A longer pregnancy counts as a bigger curse. It does not mean the animal is evil.

phrases.english: Is it written 'from all the wild animals and from all the domesticated animals'?
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: the verse does not say it in this order.

phrases.english: It is written 'from all the domesticated animals and from all the wild animals'!
phrases.notes: בראשית ג:יד, where בהמה comes first.

phrases.english: It (the snake) is cursed more than the domesticated animal
which was itself cursed more than the wild animal.
phrases.notes: This is the chain: חיה → בהמה → snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a question on the previous amud about how the derivation from the verse should run.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the order of words in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might have compared the snake directly to the חיה, or read the comparison in a different order.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse sets up a chain: the snake is compared to the בהמה, and the בהמה to the חיה.

steps.title: Why not use the goat-to-cat ratio and get fifteen months?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the derivation. It suggests the ratio could be one to three (goat compared to cat). That would give the snake only fifteen months.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: just as the domesticated animal was cursed more than the wild animal by one to three (and what case is that? a goat compared to a cat), so too the snake was cursed more than the domesticated animal by one to three, which comes to fifteen months!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why we must use the donkey's one-to-seven ratio. It points out that a goat compared to a cat gives only one to three, and that would make the snake's pregnancy fifteen months instead of seven years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cat carries about 52 days and a goat about 5 months, which is roughly one to three. The goat's 5 months times three comes to fifteen months. The challenge is that nothing in the reasoning so far forces us to pick the donkey over the goat.

keyTerms.meaning: But say instead... (introduces another possible reading)

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'ומאי ניהו? עז מחתול' are a short side-explanation inside the challenge. They are not a separate question and answer.

phrases.english: But say: just as the domesticated animal was cursed
more than the wild animal by one to three,
and what is that? A goat compared to a cat,
phrases.notes: Goat: about 5 months. Cat: about 52 days.

phrases.english: so too it (the snake) was cursed more than the domesticated animal

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד לְשָׁלֹשׁ, דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ חֲמֵיסַר יַרְחֵי!
phrases.english: by one to three, which comes to fifteen months!
phrases.notes: 5 months × 3 = 15 months.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the chain from Step 1 but challenges which animals should be used to set the ratio.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of the donkey's one-to-seven ratio, which produces seven years
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The goat is also a בהמה, and its ratio to the cat is only one to three. Using it gives fifteen months, so the seven-year figure is not forced.

steps.title: First answer: 'all the animals' includes the most cursed one
steps.stepSummary: The verse says 'from all the בהמה'. This means the snake is cursed more than every domesticated animal, including the donkey, which has the longest pregnancy.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say: it is written 'from ALL the domesticated animals.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the word 'all' (כל) in the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'All' means the snake must be cursed more than every בהמה, not just the goat. So we must measure from the donkey, the most cursed one. That gives one to seven and seven years.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say... (introduces one of several possible answers)

phrases.english: If you wish, say: 'from ALL the domesticated animals' is written.
phrases.notes: 'All' includes the donkey, which has the greatest curse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of a word in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any בהמה, such as the goat, could be used for the ratio.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'All' requires comparing to the most cursed בהמה, the donkey, which gives seven years.

steps.title: Second answer: a curse should be given at full strength
steps.stepSummary: Since this is a curse, we read it as harshly as the verse allows. So we choose the bigger ratio.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you wish, say instead: it is a curse, so cast the heaviest curse upon it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, separate answer to the same challenge. This one is based on logic rather than a word in the verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse is cursing the snake. So when two readings are possible, we choose the harsher one: one to seven (seven years), not one to three (fifteen months).

keyTerms.meaning: Or if you wish, say... (introduces an alternative answer)

steps.whatToRemember: The snake's seven-year pregnancy is defended in two ways: (1) 'from ALL the animals' includes the donkey, and (2) a curse is read at its heaviest.

phrases.english: Or if you wish, say: it is a curse,
so place the (full) curse upon it.
phrases.notes: Choose the harsher ratio.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to the challenge in Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical principle (a curse is applied with full force)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The milder one-to-three ratio could apply.
steps.terutzMaskana: A curse is given its fullest measure, so the ratio is one to seven.

steps.title: The emperor asks how long a snake carries its young
steps.stepSummary: The קיסר asks רבי יהושע בן חנניה how long a snake is pregnant before giving birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: The emperor said to רבי יהושע בן חנניה: A snake, after how long does it give birth?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story on the same topic of a snake's pregnancy. This line sets up the question that the story will discuss.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story moves from deriving the number out of the verse to a real-world challenge. It tests whether the seven years from the verse matches what people have observed.

phrases.english: The emperor said to
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya:
A snake, after how long is it pregnant and gives birth?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ קֵיסָר לְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story on the same topic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How long a snake's pregnancy lasts

steps.title: רבי יהושע answers: seven years
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that a snake gives birth after seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: After seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives his answer: seven years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His answer matches the number derived from the verse. This gives the emperor a clear claim to challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: He said to him: After seven years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 5.

steps.title: The Athens experiment: they gave birth after three years
steps.stepSummary: The emperor says the elders of Athens bred snakes, and the snakes gave birth after only three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the elders of Athens mated them, and they gave birth after three years!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor challenges the seven-year answer with a real experiment. In it, snakes gave birth after just three years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a challenge from observation. If snakes were mated and gave birth three years later, it looks like the pregnancy is three years, not seven.

keyTerms.meaning: They mated them (caused them to breed)

phrases.english: But the elders of Athens mated them,
and they gave birth after three (years)!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a snake's pregnancy is seven years
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An observed experiment showed birth three years after mating.

steps.title: They were already pregnant for four years
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that those snakes were already four years into their pregnancy before the experiment began.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those snakes had already been pregnant for four years beforehand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע explains away the experiment. The snakes were already pregnant when the experiment started.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four years before the experiment plus three years during it equals seven years. So the experiment does not contradict the seven-year answer.

phrases.english: Those were already pregnant from beforehand, for four (years).
phrases.notes: 4 + 3 = 7 years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the facts of the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The pregnancy began when the experiment began.
steps.terutzMaskana: The pregnancy began four years earlier, so the total is still seven years.

steps.title: But they mated, which shows they weren't pregnant yet
steps.stepSummary: The emperor objects that the snakes mated during the experiment. Animals only mate when they are not already pregnant.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they engaged in mating!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor pushes back on רבי יהושע's answer. If the snakes were already pregnant, why did they mate?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption is that animals mate only in order to reproduce. Mating would then prove the snakes were not yet pregnant, which brings back the three-year problem.

phrases.english: But they were engaging in mating!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the snakes were already pregnant
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Animals do not mate while pregnant, so mating shows the pregnancy had not yet begun.

steps.title: Snakes mate like people, even when pregnant
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that snakes mate like humans do. They do not mate only to reproduce.
steps.simpleTranslation: They also engage in mating like people.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the last challenge. Snakes, like people, mate even when they are already pregnant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This removes the emperor's assumption that mating proves an animal is not pregnant. The four-year head start still stands, and so does the seven-year pregnancy.
steps.whatToRemember: The seven-year snake pregnancy holds up. The Athens experiment is explained by an earlier four-year start, and snakes mate like humans, even while pregnant.

phrases.english: They also engage in mating like people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 9 and closes the exchange.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Animals mate only when they are not pregnant.
steps.terutzMaskana: Snakes mate like humans, so mating does not prove they were not already pregnant.

steps.title: The emperor asks: aren't the Athenian sages wise?
steps.stepSummary: The emperor challenges רבי יהושע for contradicting the respected sages of Athens.
steps.simpleTranslation: But aren't they wise men?
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor pushes back. How can רבי יהושע reject the Athenian experiment when the people who ran it are famous wise men?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the debate was about the facts of snake pregnancy. Now the emperor stops arguing about snakes and appeals to authority instead. The new question is whose wisdom can be trusted.

phrases.english: But aren't they wise?
phrases.notes: Spoken by the emperor about the elders of Athens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רבי יהושע's last answer by questioning his right to disagree with the Athenians.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's rejection of the Athenian experiment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Athenians are recognized as wise, so their findings should outweigh his claim.

steps.title: רבי יהושע: we are wiser than they are
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that the Jewish sages are wiser than the Athenians.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are wiser than they are.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the challenge directly. Yes, they are wise, but we are wiser.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not deny that the Athenians are wise. He claims a higher level of wisdom for the חכמי ישראל. That bold claim sets up the dare that comes next.

phrases.english: We are wiser than they are.
phrases.notes: Spoken by רבי יהושע.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the emperor's appeal to the Athenians' authority.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Athenians' wisdom settles the question.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Jewish sages are wiser, so the Athenians' view is not final.

steps.title: The emperor dares him to defeat them
steps.stepSummary: The emperor tells רבי יהושע to prove his claim by beating the Athenian sages and bringing them back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you are wiser, go defeat them and bring them to me!
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor turns רבי יהושע's claim into a dare: prove it. This sets up the whole journey to Athens that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words are not enough for the emperor. He wants proof he can see: the Athenian sages beaten and brought to him. The rest of the story is how רבי יהושע meets this demand.

phrases.english: If you are wiser,
go defeat them and bring them to me!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי חֲכִימַתְּ, זִיל זַכִּינְהוּ וְאַיְתִינְהוּ לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim of step 12 by demanding proof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim 'we are wiser than they.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A claim of greater wisdom has to be shown in practice.

steps.title: How many sages are there?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע accepts the dare and asks how many Athenian sages there are.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: How many are there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע does not back down. He asks a practical question to start planning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By asking for the number, he shows he accepts the challenge. The answer will decide how he gets ready for the trip.

phrases.english: He said to him: How many are there?
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע speaking.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the dare and asks for a planning detail.

steps.title: There are sixty men
steps.stepSummary: The emperor answers that there are sixty sages.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sixty men.
steps.whatsHappening: The emperor gives the number: sixty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number sixty matters right away. רבי יהושע will build his preparations around it.

phrases.english: Sixty men.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.

steps.title: A ship with sixty rooms and sixty mattresses each
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע has the emperor build a ship with sixty rooms, each holding sixty mattresses, and the emperor builds it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Make me a ship with sixty rooms, and in each room sixty mattresses. He made it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע prepares to bring all sixty sages back. He asks for a ship with a room for each sage, and the emperor provides it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ship shows he fully expects to win and bring the sages home. The sixty mattresses in each room look strange now; Step 58 shows what they are for.

phrases.english: He said to him: Make me a ship
that has sixty rooms in it,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֹל בֵּיתָא אִית בַּהּ שִׁיתִּין בִּיסְתַּרְקֵי.
phrases.english: and each room has sixty mattresses in it.
He (the emperor) made it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the number sixty from step 15 to prepare for the journey.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע prepares a ship big enough to bring back all sixty sages.

steps.title: Buying the butcher's 'head'
steps.stepSummary: In Athens, רבי יהושע asks a butcher whether his head is for sale. The butcher says yes, for half a זוז, and רבי יהושע pays him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he arrived there, at a butcher shop, he found a man skinning an animal. He said to him: Is your head for sale? He said: Yes. He said: For how much? He said: For half a זוז. He gave it to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע reaches Athens and sets a verbal trap. He asks the butcher about 'your head,' and the butcher thinks he means the animal's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'your head' (רֵישָׁךְ) can mean the butcher's own head or the animal head he is selling. The butcher hears the ordinary meaning and accepts payment. רבי יהושע will now use the literal meaning against him.

phrases.english: When he arrived there, at a butcher shop,
he found a certain man
who was skinning an animal.
He said to him: Is your head for sale?
phrases.notes: Deliberately unclear: the butcher's own head, or the head he sells.

phrases.english: He said to him: Yes.
He said to him: For how much?
He said to him: For half a zuz.
He gave it (the money) to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The journey begins. רבי יהושע arrives in Athens and sets a trap.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע 'buys' the butcher's head using wording with two meanings.

steps.title: Springing the trap: show me the school
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע claims he bought the butcher's own head, not the animal's. He offers to let him go if the butcher shows him the entrance to the Athenian sages' school.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, he said to him: Did I say the animal's head to you? He said to him: If you want me to let you go, go show me the entrance to the school of Athens.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע springs his trap. He 'owns' the butcher's head, so he uses that to get what he really needs: the hidden location of the school.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The purchase was never about meat. It gave רבי יהושע a hold over a local man who could show him a secret place. He trades the 'head' for directions.
steps.confusionAlert: Both 'אֲמַר לֵיהּ' lines here are רבי יהושע speaking, one right after the other. The butcher's alarmed reaction is left unsaid.

phrases.english: In the end, he said to him:
Did I tell you the head of the animal?
phrases.notes: In other words: I bought your own head.

phrases.english: He said to him: If you want me to let you go,

phrases.aramaic: סַגִּי אַחְוִי לִי פִּיתְחָא דְּבֵי אַתּוּנָא.
phrases.english: go show me the entrance of the school of Athens.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְסוֹף, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא רֵישָׁא דְּחֵיוְתָא אֲמַרִי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the purchase from step 17 as leverage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע trades the butcher's 'head' for the location of the sages' school.

steps.title: The butcher is afraid
steps.stepSummary: The butcher objects that anyone who reveals the school's location is killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am afraid, because anyone who shows it, they kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The butcher raises a problem. Revealing the entrance could cost him his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Athenians guard their school's location with the death penalty. That makes רבי יהושע's request dangerous, so he must find a safe way for the butcher to point it out.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am afraid,
for anyone who shows it, they kill him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to the demand in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The demand to show the entrance.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Showing the entrance openly would get the butcher killed.

steps.title: Mark it with a bundle of reeds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells the butcher to carry a bundle of reeds and set it down at the entrance, as if he were just resting.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Carry a bundle of reeds, and when you get there, stand it up like someone taking a rest.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע solves the butcher's fear. The butcher can mark the spot without pointing or saying a word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Putting down a load to rest looks completely innocent, so no one can accuse the butcher of revealing anything. Even so, the upright bundle tells רבי יהושע exactly where the door is.

phrases.english: He said to him: Carry a bundle of reeds,
and when you arrive there,
stand it up like one who is resting.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the danger raised in step 19.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The butcher can only show the entrance by openly revealing it, which would get him killed.
steps.terutzMaskana: An innocent-looking act marks the spot without any open revealing.

steps.title: Guards inside and outside the school
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע finds guards inside and outside the entrance. If footprints show someone entering, the outer guards are killed; if someone leaving, the inner guards are killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He found guards on the inside and guards on the outside. If they saw a footprint going in, they killed the outer guards, and if going out, they killed the inner guards.
steps.whatsHappening: The story describes a new obstacle. The school is guarded so tightly that no one can get in or out without being noticed. This sets up how רבי יהושע will get past them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The footprints show which way a person walked. That tells the Athenians which group of guards failed: the outer guards let someone in, and the inner guards let someone out. With their lives at stake, each group is extremely watchful.
steps.confusionAlert: The Sefaria translation adds that sand was spread on the ground. That detail is not in our text; it explains how footprints could be seen.

phrases.english: He found guards on the inside
and guards on the outside,
for if they saw a footprint that was entering —
they would kill the outer ones,
and one that was exiting — they would kill the inner ones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finding the entrance, רבי יהושע faces the guard system.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The school is protected by two groups of guards, and each is punished for any footprint going its way, so getting in or out seems impossible.

steps.title: The reversed-sandal trick eliminates all the guards
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע turns his sandal backward twice. The first set of footprints gets the inner guards killed, and the second gets the remaining guards killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He reversed his sandal, and they killed the inner guards. He reversed his sandal again, and they killed all of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The story shows how רבי יהושע uses the guards' own footprint rule against them so he can get into the school.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 21 explained the rule: footprints going out mean the inner guards are killed, and footprints going in mean the outer guards are killed. By turning his sandal around, רבי יהושע first made footprints that seemed to go out, so the inner guards were killed. Then he made footprints that seemed to go in, so the rest were killed and the entrance was left unguarded.

keyTerms.meaning: He turned it over / reversed it

phrases.english: He reversed his sandal, and they killed the inner guards,
phrases.notes: Backward footprints made it look as if someone had left the building.

phrases.english: he reversed his sandal again, and they killed all of them.
phrases.notes: Now the footprints seemed to enter, so the outer guards were killed too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the obstacle from Step 21 by turning the guards' own rule against them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By using the footprint rule cleverly, רבי יהושע removes every guard and gets inside.

steps.title: A seating dilemma: whom to greet first
steps.stepSummary: Inside, the young sages sit in the upper area and the elders sit below. רבי יהושע worries that greeting the young ones first will anger the elders.
steps.simpleTranslation: He found the young ones sitting above and the old ones below. He said: If I greet these young ones first, those old ones will kill me, because they think, 'We are better, since we are older and they are just children.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story sets up a new problem. רבי יהושע must greet the sages but does not know which group to greet first. This prepares the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you greet whoever sits in the higher place of honor first, and here that is the young sages. But the elders believe age makes them more important. So whichever group he greets first, he risks offending the other.

phrases.english: He found young ones sitting above and elders below.
phrases.notes: The upper section is the more honored place.

phrases.english: He said: If I give a greeting to these (the young ones),
phrases.notes: He would greet them first because they sit higher.

phrases.english: those (the elders) will kill me,
because they think: We are more important,
since we are much older and they are just children.
phrases.notes: קַשִּׁינַן literally means 'we are harder,' meaning 'aged.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that he is inside, a new social obstacle appears.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Greeting either group first risks offending the other.

steps.title: Greeting everyone together
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע greets the whole room at once and avoids choosing a group.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Peace to you (all).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע solves the seating problem from the previous step with one general greeting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the greeting is addressed to everyone together, neither the young sages nor the elders are put first. Nobody is insulted.

keyTerms.meaning: Peace to you (plural), a greeting to everyone

phrases.english: He said: Peace to you all.
phrases.notes: A plural greeting that does not single out either group.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the dilemma raised in Step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Avoids the dilemma by choosing neither side
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed he had to greet one group first and offend the other.
steps.terutzMaskana: A general greeting honors everyone equally.

steps.title: Explaining his purpose and accepting a contest
steps.stepSummary: The Athenian sages ask why he came. He says he is a Jewish sage who wants to learn their wisdom. They decide to test him, and he sets the stakes.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What is your business here? He said to them: I am a sage of the Jews, and I want to learn wisdom from you. They said: If so, we will ask you questions! He said to them: Fine. If you win, do whatever you want to me. If I beat you, come eat with me on my ship.
steps.whatsHappening: The story sets up a battle of wits with clear stakes. This prepares the riddles that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע presents himself as a student, but the חכמי אתונה turn it into a test of his worthiness. He accepts and adds a wager. Losing could cost him his life, while winning means they must come to his ship, which hints at how the story will continue.

phrases.english: They said to him: What is your business here?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אֲנָא חַכִּימָא דִיהוּדָאֵי אֲנָא,
phrases.english: He said to them: I am a sage of the Jews,
and I want to learn wisdom from you.
(They said:) If so, we will ask you questions!
phrases.notes: They want to test whether he is worthy.

phrases.english: He said to them: Very well,
phrases.notes: לְחַיֵּי literally means 'to life,' an expression of agreement.

phrases.aramaic: אִי זָכֵיתוּ — כֹּל דְּבָעֵיתוּ עֲבִידוּ בִּי,
phrases.english: if you win, do to me whatever you want,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי זָכֵינָא בְּכוּ — אִיכְלוּ גַּבַּאי בִּסְפִינְתָּא.
phrases.english: and if I beat you, eat with me on my ship.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the greeting, the conversation turns into a formal contest.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A riddle contest begins, and the stakes are set for both sides.

steps.title: First riddle: proposing to a greater family after rejection
steps.stepSummary: The Athenians ask why a man who was refused a wife would go and propose to an even more important family.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: A certain man went and asked for a woman's hand, and they would not give her to him. Why would he think of going to a place that is even higher than him?
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenian sages ask their first test question, which looks like it has no sensible answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea behind the riddle is that if a lower family rejected him, aiming higher seems pointless and foolish. They are checking whether רבי יהושע can defend something that looks illogical.

keyTerms.meaning: (A family) that is higher than him

phrases.english: They said to him: A certain man

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָזֵיל וּבָעֵי אִתְּתָא וְלָא יָהֲבוּ לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: who went and asked for a woman, and they did not give her to him,
what does he see in going
to a place that is higher than him?
phrases.notes: Meaning a more important family.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: הַהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּאָזֵיל וּבָעֵי אִתְּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first question of the contest set up in Step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why would a rejected suitor try a more important family?

steps.title: The peg demonstration: success can be found higher up
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע pushes a peg into the low part of a wall, where it does not go in, and then into the high part, where it does. Likewise, the rejected man may find his destined match higher up.
steps.simpleTranslation: He took a peg and pushed it into the lower part of the wall, and it did not go in. He pushed it into the upper part, and it went in. He said: This man, too, may happen to find the woman destined for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the riddle with a demonstration instead of only words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The peg failed down low but succeeded higher up, where there was an opening. In the same way, failing with one family does not mean he will fail with a higher one, because a match depends on finding the one meant for him (בת מזלו), not on rank.

keyTerms.meaning: He stuck it in / pushed it in
The woman destined for him (his match)

steps.whatToRemember: The Athenians' riddles are answered with clever, concrete demonstrations. The first one teaches that being rejected in one place does not stop a man from finding his destined match somewhere else, even somewhere 'higher.'

phrases.english: He took a peg,
pushed it into the lower part, and it did not go in,
into the upper part, and it went in.
phrases.notes: There was an opening higher up in the wall.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: הַאי נָמֵי מִיתְרְמֵי בַּת מַזָּלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: He said: This man too may happen upon his destined match.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the riddle asked in Step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Just as the peg went in higher up after failing below, the man may find his destined wife in a higher family.

steps.title: Why lend again after losing money?
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask why a man who lent money and had to seize property to get paid back would ever lend again.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man lends money and ends up having to seize the borrower's property. Why would he lend again?
steps.whatsHappening: חכמי אתונה ask a new test question. It is about human behavior: why someone repeats something that went badly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question has the same shape as the earlier marriage question in Step 26. Someone had a bad experience. Why would he try again? Collecting a loan by seizing property is a hassle and a risk, so lending again seems foolish.

keyTerms.meaning: seizes property to collect a debt
what did he see, meaning why would he?
again, he went back and did it

phrases.english: A man who lends and then has to seize property,
phrases.notes: The borrower did not pay, so the lender had to collect from property.

phrases.english: why would he go and lend again?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next test question after the marriage riddle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason a burned lender keeps lending.

steps.title: The bundle of reeds: keep going until help comes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע compares the lender to a man who cuts a load too heavy to lift. He keeps adding to it until someone comes along to help him raise it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man went to the marsh and cut a bundle but could not lift it. So he kept cutting and piling more on top, until a person happened by and lifted it up for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers with a picture from daily life. People keep trying, expecting that eventually things will work out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man does not give up when the first load is too heavy. He keeps working, trusting that a helper will come. In the same way, the lender keeps lending, expecting to find a good borrower in the end. One failure does not stop a reasonable person.

keyTerms.meaning: marsh, pond area where reeds grow

phrases.english: He said to them:
A man went to the marsh,

phrases.aramaic: קְטַל קַמָּא טוּנָא וְלָא מָצֵי בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: first he cut a bundle, but could not lift it,
so he cuts more and places it on top,
until a person happens by and lifts it for him.
phrases.notes: The two bracketed spellings are textual variants of the same word.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the lending question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: People keep trying because they expect a good outcome to come eventually, just like the reed-cutter who waits for a helper.

steps.title: Tell us some nonsense
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה demand that רבי יהושע tell them something made-up and absurd.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Tell us some nonsense!
steps.whatsHappening: This is a new kind of test. They ask for nonsense, and this sets up his clever story in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trap is that anything he says can be attacked. If he tells a story they accept as possible, he failed to give nonsense. If he speaks foolishly, he looks foolish.

phrases.english: They said to him:
Tell us words of nonsense!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge in the contest.

steps.title: The mule that gave birth with an IOU
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells of a mule that gave birth. The baby wore a note saying it was owed 100,000 זוז by its father's family.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a mule that gave birth. A note hung on the baby, and it said the baby was owed 100,000 זוז by its father's household.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives the requested nonsense as a story that sounds detailed and serious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story is told in a normal, factual style. That style tempts the listeners to react as if it were real. A mule is a sterile animal, so the story is impossible from its very first detail.

keyTerms.meaning: a note or slip of writing

phrases.english: He said to them:
There was a certain mule that gave birth,
and a note was hanging on it,
and written on it was that it is owed by its father's household
one hundred thousand zuz.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fulfills the demand for nonsense.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A story that is impossible from the very start: a mule giving birth.

steps.title: But mules can't give birth!
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה object that a mule cannot give birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Does a mule give birth?
steps.whatsHappening: חכמי אתונה fall into the trap and point out that the story is impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They treat the story as if it should be realistic and attack it for being impossible. Without meaning to, they have admitted that it is nonsense, which is exactly what they asked for.

keyTerms.meaning: does it give birth? (said with surprise)

phrases.english: They said to him:
But does a mule give birth?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the story told in Step 31.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mules are sterile, so the story cannot be true.

steps.title: That's exactly the nonsense you asked for
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע replies that the impossibility is the whole point. This is the nonsense they requested.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: These are the words of nonsense!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע turns their objection into proof that he passed the test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their objection proves the story is nonsense. So the objection itself shows he did exactly what they asked.

phrases.english: He said to them:
These are the words of nonsense.
phrases.notes: The two bracketed readings are textual variants with the same meaning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the objection from Step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turning the challenge into proof of success.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The impossibility seemed to be a flaw in the story.
steps.terutzMaskana: The impossibility is exactly what makes it the nonsense they asked for.

steps.title: How do you salt spoiled salt?
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask what you use to preserve salt once it has spoiled.
steps.simpleTranslation: When salt spoils, what do you salt it with?
steps.whatsHappening: A new trick question. It assumes something impossible, that salt can spoil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Salt is what we use to preserve other things, so the question has no real answer. It is a trap built on a false assumption.

phrases.english: Salt, when it spoils,
with what does one salt it?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְחָא כִּי סָרְיָא, בְּמַאי מָלְחִי לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new trick question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to preserve salt that has spoiled.

steps.title: With a mule's afterbirth
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers: salt it with the placenta of a mule.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: With the placenta of a mule.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע gives an impossible answer on purpose. This sets up the exchange in the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mule does not give birth, so it has no placenta. He answers an impossible question with an impossible answer.

phrases.english: He said to them:
With the placenta of a mule.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the salt question.

steps.title: Does a mule even have a placenta?
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה object that a mule has no placenta.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there such a thing as a mule's placenta?
steps.whatsHappening: חכמי אתונה attack his answer because it is impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words "they said to him" are not written here, but the speakers are clearly חכמי אתונה. They catch the impossibility in his answer and miss the one in their own question.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse the speakers. Step 36 is the Athenians' objection, and Step 37 is רבי יהושע's comeback, even though the text does not say who is talking.

phrases.english: But is there a placenta for a mule?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in Step 35.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mules do not give birth, so they have no placenta.

steps.title: Does salt even spoil?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע fires back: and does salt spoil?
steps.simpleTranslation: And does salt spoil?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע shows that his answer was as impossible as their question, on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His point is that an impossible question deserves an impossible answer. Their objection to his answer applies just as much to their own question.
steps.whatToRemember: In these riddles רבי יהושע beats trick questions by matching them. He answers nonsense with nonsense, which exposes the false assumption hidden in the question.

phrases.english: And does salt spoil?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in Step 36 by turning it back on the original question.
steps.terutzMaskana: Their question was just as absurd, so an absurd answer fits it.

steps.title: Build us a house in midair
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה demand that רבי יהושע build them a house in the open air.
steps.simpleTranslation: Build us a house in the air of the world!
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge. This time it is an impossible task, not a question to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the riddles, this asks him to actually do something impossible. It sets up his surprising response.

keyTerms.meaning: the open air of the world

phrases.english: Build us a house
in the air of the world!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new impossible demand.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: That he build a house in midair.

steps.title: He hovers in the air and asks for bricks
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע says a Divine Name, floats between sky and earth, and tells them to bring up bricks and mortar.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said a Divine Name and hung between the sky and the earth. He said to them: Bring me up bricks and mortar.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע accepts the challenge. He puts himself in the air and hands the impossible part back to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is ready to build in midair, but they cannot get the materials up to him. So the failure becomes theirs, not his.

phrases.english: He said a Divine Name,
and hung between the sky and the earth.
He said to them:
Bring up to me bricks and mortar.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שֵׁם, תְּלָא בֵּין רְקִיעָא לְאַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the house-in-the-air demand.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is ready to build in midair. Supplying the materials is their job, and they cannot do it.

steps.title: Where is the center of the world?
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask where the exact middle of the world is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where is the middle of the world?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question with no answer anyone could check. It sets up his clever reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one can easily prove where the world's center is, so any answer he gives seems open to attack.

phrases.english: Where is the middle of the world?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new test question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The location of the world's center.

steps.title: Right here
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע raises his finger and says: here.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised his finger and said to them: Here.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע simply points and says the center is right where he is standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since no one can easily disprove it, any spot works as an answer. This sets up their objection.

phrases.english: He raised his finger,
and said to them: Here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the center-of-the-world question.

steps.title: Who says so?
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה challenge: who says you are right?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: And who says so?
steps.whatsHappening: חכמי אתונה demand proof for his claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They attack his answer because nothing supports it.

keyTerms.meaning: who says? who can prove it?

phrases.english: They said to him:
And who says?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'here' is the center.

steps.title: Bring ropes and measure
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע tells them to bring ropes and measure for themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bring ropes and measure!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע puts the burden of proof back on them. If they think he is wrong, let them measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measuring the whole world is impossible, so they can never disprove him. He wins by showing that their demand for proof cannot be met by either side.
steps.whatToRemember: In all these tests רבי יהושע wins the same way. He accepts the challenge on his own terms and hands the impossible part back to the challengers.

phrases.english: Bring ropes and measure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the demand for proof in Step 42.
steps.terutzMaskana: They cannot disprove him without measuring the world, which no one can do.

steps.title: Bring the pit from the field into the city
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה demand that רבי יהושע move a pit from the field into the city.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a pit in the field; bring it into the city!
steps.whatsHappening: חכמי אתונה give רבי יהושע a new impossible task. They ask him to move a hole in the ground into town.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit is just empty space dug into the ground, so it cannot be picked up and carried. The demand is meant to trap him with something that cannot be done.

phrases.english: We have a pit in the field,
bring it into the city!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the measuring challenge, the Athenians move to a new impossible task.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can an immovable pit be carried into the city?

steps.title: Braid me ropes of bran
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע agrees to move the pit if they first braid him ropes out of bran.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Braid ropes of bran for me, and I will bring it in.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers by asking them for something just as impossible: ropes made from loose bran.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bran is crumbly flakes and cannot be twisted into rope. By making his help depend on an impossible condition, he shows that their demand is just as absurd.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Braid ropes of bran for me
and I will bring it in.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אַפְשִׁילוּ לִי חַבְלֵי מִפָּארֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the pit demand.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An impossible demand is met with an equally impossible condition.

steps.title: Sew up the broken millstone
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה demand that רבי יהושע sew a broken millstone back together.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a mill that broke; sew it!
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians give another impossible task: stitch a stone mill back together like cloth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A millstone is solid stone, so no needle and thread can repair it. The trap works the same way as the pit.

phrases.english: We have a mill that is broken;
sew it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new impossible task, built the same way as the pit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How can a stone mill be sewn?

steps.title: Pull threads out of the stone for me
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע agrees to sew the mill if they first pull threads out of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Pull out threads from it for me, and I will sew it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע again answers with an impossible condition: give me threads drawn from the stone itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the mill could be sewn, it would need thread, and stone has no threads to pull. His answer exposes that their request makes no sense.

phrases.english: He said:
Pull out threads from it for me
and I will sew it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the millstone demand.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Bring threads made of the stone, and I will sew it with them.

steps.title: How do you harvest a field of knives
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask what tool you use to harvest a field where knives grow.
steps.simpleTranslation: A field of knives, with what do they harvest it?
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians ask a riddle about an imaginary field where knives grow like grain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes something that does not exist. They want to see whether he will get stuck trying to answer it seriously.

phrases.english: A field of knives,
with what do they harvest it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new riddle.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What tool harvests a field of knives?

steps.title: With a donkey's horn
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that you harvest it with the horn of a donkey.
steps.simpleTranslation: With the horn of a donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע names a tool that does not exist, since donkeys have no horns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He gives an answer as imaginary as the question. This sets them up to object, and their objection will turn against them.

phrases.english: With the horn of a donkey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the field-of-knives riddle.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A non-existent tool for a non-existent field.

steps.title: But a donkey has no horn
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה object that donkeys do not have horns.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is there such a thing as a horn on a donkey?
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians attack his answer by pointing out that a donkey's horn does not exist.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their objection is correct, but it falls into his trap. By complaining that his answer is imaginary, they admit that imaginary things are not acceptable.

keyTerms.meaning: but is there? (a challenge asking whether something really exists)

phrases.english: But is there a horn on a donkey?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 49.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The tool he named does not exist.

steps.title: And is there a field of knives
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע turns their objection back on them: a field of knives does not exist either.
steps.simpleTranslation: And is there such a thing as a field of knives?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע uses the very same words to show that their question was just as imaginary as his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He repeats their phrase וּמִי אִיכָּא word for word, flipping the challenge around. An imaginary question deserves an imaginary answer, so their objection collapses.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהושע's main strategy in this story: when a question or demand rests on something impossible, he answers in the same impossible terms and exposes the absurdity.

phrases.english: And is there a field of knives?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the objection of step 50 back against the questioners.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turning the challenge back on the challenger
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His answer seems invalid because it names something that does not exist.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question itself was about something that does not exist, so an imaginary answer fits it.

steps.title: Which egg came from the black hen
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה bring two eggs and ask which came from a black hen and which from a white hen.
steps.simpleTranslation: They brought him two eggs and said to him: Which is from a black hen and which is from a white hen?
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians test him with two eggs that look alike and ask him to tell which hen laid each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An egg shows no sign of the color of the hen that laid it. They are asking for information that cannot be known by looking.

phrases.english: They brought him two eggs,
they said to him:
Which is from a black hen
and which is from a white hen?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new test, this time with physical objects.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Identify which hen laid each egg.

steps.title: Which cheese came from the black goat
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע brings two cheeses and asks which came from a black goat and which from a white goat.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought them two cheeses and said to them: Which is from the black goat and which is from the white goat?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers with a matching test: two cheeses whose source animal cannot be identified either.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as cheese gives no sign of the goat's color, an egg gives no sign of the hen's color. His counter-question shows that their question has no answer.

phrases.english: He brought them two cheeses,
he said to them:
Which is from the black goat
and which is from the white goat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the egg test with a parallel cheese test.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A parallel unanswerable question shows that the original question cannot be answered.

steps.title: How does a chick's spirit leave a sealed egg
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask where the spirit of a chick that dies inside its egg goes out.
steps.simpleTranslation: A chick that died, from where does its spirit go out?
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians ask how the life-spirit of a chick that dies inside an unbroken egg could leave, since the shell is sealed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shell has no opening, so the question seems to have no answer. It is the setup for his short reply.

phrases.english: A chick that died,
from where does its spirit go out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new riddle, still connected to eggs.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How does a spirit leave a sealed egg?

steps.title: It leaves the way it came in
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע answers that the spirit leaves the same way it entered.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where it entered, it went out.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers that the spirit went out the same way it came in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirit entered the sealed egg without any opening. So there is no difficulty in it leaving without an opening either.

keyTerms.meaning: from where it entered, it exited

phrases.english: From where it entered, it went out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the chick riddle.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The spirit entered without a hole, so it can leave without one.

steps.title: Show us an object not worth its damage
steps.stepSummary: חכמי אתונה ask him to show them an object that causes more loss than it is worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Show us a utensil that is not worth the damage it causes!
steps.whatsHappening: The Athenians challenge him to produce, in real life, an item whose damage is greater than its value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time they want a demonstration, not a clever line. It sets up the practical trick in the next step.

phrases.english: Show us a utensil
that is not worth its damage!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחְוִי לַן מָנָא דְּלָא שָׁוֵי חֲבִילֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge that asks for a demonstration.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A real example of an object whose damage outweighs its value.

steps.title: The mat that forced them to break the gate
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע has them spread out mats that are too wide for the gate, then tells them to break the gate. A cheap mat thus causes expensive damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Each one brought a mat and spread it out. It did not fit through the gate. He said to them: Bring axes and break it down. This is a utensil that is not worth its damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע acts out the answer. Each of them spreads out a mat, the mats are too wide for the gate, and he tells them to smash the gate to bring the mats in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mat is worth very little, but breaking down a gate is a large loss. The demonstration proves his point in front of their own eyes, and the last line states the lesson.
steps.whatToRemember: Every challenge here follows the same pattern. Absurd demands get absurd counter-demands, unanswerable riddles get parallel riddles, and the final challenge is answered by a live demonstration.

phrases.english: Each and every one brought a mat,
spread it out.
It would not go in through the gate.
He said to them:
Bring axes, break it down.
This is a utensil that is not worth its damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Meets the demand of step 56 with a practical demonstration.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A cheap mat that forces the breaking of a gate is an object not worth the damage it causes.

steps.title: Each sage is placed in a room and assumes his friends are coming
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע brings each of חכמי אתונה onto the ship. Each one sees sixty mattresses and thinks all his colleagues are coming to join him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought each and every one of them in. When each one saw sixty mattresses, he said: 'All my colleagues are coming here.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. Having won the contest, רבי יהושע leads each of חכמי אתונה into his own room on the ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each room was prepared with sixty mattresses. Seeing so many places to sit, each sage concluded that his whole group would gather in his room, so he sat and waited instead of growing suspicious. This keeps them calm and in place while the ship gets ready to leave.
steps.confusionAlert: The sixty mattresses are not an extra detail. רבי יהושע set them up on purpose so each sage would think his friends were on their way and would not try to leave.

phrases.english: He brought them, each and every one,
phrases.notes: Each sage was led into a separate room on the ship.

phrases.english: when he saw sixty mattresses,
phrases.notes: Each sage saw the sixty mattresses in his own room.

phrases.english: he said: All my colleagues
phrases.notes: He said this to himself.

phrases.english: are coming here.
phrases.notes: So he waited calmly instead of leaving.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the final riddle (Step 57), the debate is over and רבי יהושע begins carrying out his plan to take the sages away.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sages are tricked into staying calmly in their rooms, each one thinking his friends are coming.

steps.title: רבי יהושע tells the sailor to set sail
steps.stepSummary: With the sages settled in their rooms, רבי יהושע orders the sailor to release the ship.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to the sailor: 'Release your ship.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the sages are waiting quietly, רבי יהושע tells the sailor to start sailing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plan works. The sages do not notice anything wrong, so the ship can leave Athens without any struggle. They are now being carried toward the emperor.

phrases.english: He said to the sailor:
phrases.notes: רבי יהושע is speaking.

phrases.english: Release your ship.
phrases.notes: In other words, untie it and start sailing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Because the trick in Step 58 kept the sages calm, the ship can now leave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ship sets sail with the sages on board.

steps.title: On the way, רבי יהושע takes earth from their homeland
steps.stepSummary: As they travel, רבי יהושע takes some earth from the soil of Athens. This sets up a later part of the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: While they were traveling, he took some earth from their earth.
steps.whatsHappening: During the voyage, רבי יהושע takes some earth from the land of Athens. This step sets up a later scene where the earth will be used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The detail seems minor, but it is a setup. The story will soon show why רבי יהושע needed earth from the sages' homeland once they arrived at the emperor's court. For now, just note that he has it with him.

keyTerms.meaning: While they were coming or traveling

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהושע beat חכמי אתונה with his wits. He kept them calm with the sixty mattresses, sailed off, and brought earth from their homeland. That earth will matter later in the story.

phrases.english: While they were coming,
phrases.notes: That is, during the trip toward the emperor.

phrases.english: he took earth from their earth.
phrases.notes: Soil from the sages' home city of Athens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the voyage that began in Step 59 and adds a detail that prepares the next scene.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע takes earth from Athens to use later in the story.
